cluster_name: US aviation sanctions ground Iranian flights to Baghdad and Muscat
event_summary: On September 23, Iranian airlines cancelled flights to Baghdad, Muscat, Qatar, Georgia, and Azerbaijan as US Treasury secondary sanctions took effect. Turkish Airlines, AJet, and Pegasus had suspended all Iran services through March 2027 after OFAC revoked General License J-1 on September 8.
tldr: The most striking detail is that Mahan Air completed a flight to Guangzhou hours after US secondary sanctions took effect, with China publicly declaring the measures “illegal” — a direct test of US enforcement reach against a non-allied major power. Simultaneously on September 22, US envoy Steve Witkoff met Iranian Foreign Minister Araqchi at UNGA, oil fell below $100 on news of “very productive” talks, and President Pezeshkian flew to New York on Ashianeh, an obscure carrier not yet on any sanctions list — the aviation pressure and a diplomatic track ran in parallel on the same day. Turkey’s three major carriers all suspended Iran routes through March 2027, illustrating how the US-origin aircraft parts rule creates near-total compliance from fleet-dependent allies. The Iraq–China split — Baghdad complying while Beijing defied — provides the first real-world test of whether US secondary sanctions can enforce a global shutdown of Iranian civil aviation.

evidence.quote:
The suspensions followed a Sep 8 decision by the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to indefinitely suspend General License J-1.
The license had allowed foreign airlines to temporarily bring US-made aircraft, or aircraft containing significant amounts of US-origin parts and technology, into Iran. It enabled carriers to operate Airbus and Boeing aircraft on Iranian routes.
Its suspension exposed airlines whose fleets consist entirely of such aircraft to potential US sanctions.

silences.what_they_covered_instead: No Iraqi outlet present despite Baghdad being the most-cited cancelled destination; Baghdad officials are quoted via AFP as planning to comply, but Iraqi media perspectives on the compliance decision are absent.
Dubai is mentioned as a route still operating, making the UAE a direct stakeholder, but no Gulf media outlet covered the sanctions or the Dubai exemption angle.
Russia operates competing Eurasian air corridors to Iran and has itself faced Western secondary-sanctions pressure; its absence leaves the Russia-Iran aviation relationship unexamined.

single_outlet_findings.finding: President Pezeshkian reached New York for UNGA on Ashianeh, a little-known Iranian carrier not yet on US or EU sanctions lists — the government itself found a compliance loophole for the presidential flight.

Iranian hard-liners demanded impeachment proceedings against Pezeshkian after Witkoff met Araqchi at UNGA on September 22 — the aviation sanctions are running in parallel with an active domestic political crisis over engaging with Washington.

Oil fell below $100 per barrel on September 23 after Trump described US-Iran UNGA talks as very productive — the market interpreted the diplomatic signal as softening the economic D-Day threat on the same day sanctions took effect.

All three of Turkey’s major carriers (Turkish Airlines, AJet, Pegasus) suspended Iran routes through at least March 2027 because their fleets depend entirely on US-origin aircraft — the General License J-1 revocation is a near-complete lever over Boeing/Airbus-dependent airlines.

An Iranian Mahan Air flight landed in Guangzhou after secondary sanctions took effect per FlightRadar24 — the first documented instance of a sanctioned Iranian carrier completing an international flight under the new enforcement regime.

State media covers the story entirely through China’s rejection of sanctions, omitting domestic flight cancellations or traveler disruption — a near-complete reframe of the same events covered across the rest of the corpus.

Turkey’s suspension is framed specifically around cutting off a key affordable hub for Iranians, emphasising that the squeeze falls heaviest on ordinary travelers rather than regime figures who can use obscure unblacklisted carriers.

bottom_line: US secondary aviation sanctions produced split compliance on day one: Turkey and regional neighbors folded immediately while China openly defied the measures, with a Mahan Air flight landing in Guangzhou as proof. The deepest irony is that while Bessent threatened a global shutdown of Iranian carriers, the Iranian president flew to New York the same day on an unblacklisted carrier, and US-Iran talks at UNGA pushed oil below $100 — coercion and negotiation ran in parallel.
